title: Beef Olives
subtitle: Thin beef slices rolled around a herb stuffing and braised in gravy
excerpt: Beef olives are a traditional British braised dish: thin slices of beef topside or silverside rolled tightly around a herb and breadcrumb stuffing, then braised slowly in beef stock until tender. The name has nothing to do with olive fruit , the rolls were once called olives because of their shape. They are a dish of frugal ingenuity from British farmhouse cooking.
sourceNotes: Beef olives appear in British cookbooks from the seventeenth century onwards. The term derives from the old French alouette (lark), referring to a small meat bundle in the shape of a rolled bird. The dish was a way of making a small amount of meat go further through the addition of a bread-based stuffing.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze after braising and cooling. Defrost overnight and reheat at 160°C fan, covered, for 30 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Braise the day before and refrigerate. Reheat gently to serve.

content.text: Beef olives are a patient dish: the preparation is careful (the beef must be pounded thin and rolled tightly around the stuffing), but the braising is largely unsupervised. The stuffing expands slightly as it cooks and absorbs the braising juices, which makes the filling moist and savoury. Tie each roll with kitchen string or secure with a cocktail stick: they must not unravel during braising.

items.prepNote: cut into 8 thin slices and pounded flat to about 5 mm
slices, crust removed, made into fine crumbs

content.text: Make and roll the beef olives
Fry the lardons briefly until they render their fat. Mix with the grated onion, sage, thyme, breadcrumbs, and melted butter. Season. The stuffing should hold together when pressed.
Lay the pounded beef slices flat. Place a small mound of stuffing in the centre of each. Roll tightly and tie with kitchen string or secure with a cocktail stick.

Heat the oven to 160°C fan. Brown the beef rolls in a Dutch oven over high heat, turning carefully. Set aside. Cook the sliced onion and carrot for 5 minutes in the same pot. Add the tomato puree and cook for 1 minute. Return the beef rolls and pour over {{stock-beef}} of beef stock with {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce.
Cover and braise for 1.5 hours until the beef is tender. Remove the string. Strain the braising liquid and reduce on the hob to a glossy gravy. Season and pour over the beef olives to serve.

items.symptom: The rolls have come apart during braising
items.cause: They were not secured tightly enough.
items.fix: Tie each roll with at least two pieces of string , one around the middle and one lengthways if the roll is thick. Tie them tightly before browning.

items.symptom: The stuffing is dry and crumbling
items.cause: Not enough fat in the stuffing, or the breadcrumbs were too dry.
items.fix: The lardons provide fat and the melted butter binds the mixture. If it still seems dry, add a small beaten egg to the stuffing before rolling.

items.symptom: The beef is still chewy after 1.5 hours
items.cause: The slices were too thick, or the cut was not ideal for braising.
items.fix: The slices need to be pounded to about 5 mm. A thicker piece will not become tender in 90 minutes. Alternatively, continue braising for 30 more minutes.

items.symptom: The gravy is thin and watery
items.fix: Reduce the strained braising liquid over high heat for 5 to 10 minutes. It should coat the back of a spoon.

content.text: Beef olives are one of the oldest dishes in the British cannon, documented from the seventeenth century as a way of stretching a small amount of good meat. They appear in farmhouse cookbooks from every century between 1600 and the 1950s, then largely disappeared from British home cooking as the food culture shifted. They are worth reviving: the result is a generous, flavourful dish that looks impressive for the amount of effort involved.
